claims.text: Incorporating lightweight elements such as aluminum or titanium into a high-entropy alloy induces controlled lattice distortion.
The induced lattice distortion increases mechanical strength through solid-solution strengthening.
Incorporation of the lightweight elements promotes formation of a robust, self-healing passivating oxide film.
The combined strengthening and passivation effects enable low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance to be achieved simultaneously.
The baseline high-entropy alloy lacking targeted lightweight-element substitutions has a higher density than the substituted alloy.
Replacing a portion of heavier constituents with lightweight elements reduces the alloy's overall density.
Atomic-size disparity introduced by lightweight-element substitution increases lattice strain.
The increased lattice strain reinforces the alloy through solid-solution strengthening.
Lattice strain alters the alloy's surface chemistry and defect distribution.
The altered surface chemistry and defect distribution facilitate formation of a uniform protective oxide film.
The protective oxide film improves corrosion resistance.
The protective oxide film improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Within an optimal composition window, the lightweight-substituted alloy will have mechanical strength comparable to or greater than the baseline alloy.
Within an optimal composition window, the lightweight-substituted alloy will have superior corrosion resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
Within an optimal composition window, the lightweight-substituted alloy will have superior high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
Exceeding the optimum lightweight-element concentration can cause phase instability, including undesirable intermetallic formation.
Extremely high temperatures or sufficiently aggressive oxidizing media can overwhelm the self-healing capacity of the passivating film.
